## Overview

Backpressure in a streaming pipeline is the mechanism by which a slow downstream consumer signals an upstream producer to reduce its emission rate, rather than letting an unbounded buffer grow until the process runs out of memory.

Without backpressure, a fast producer can fill memory buffers faster than a slow consumer can drain them, eventually leading to out-of-memory errors. Backpressure ensures that the system operates at the pace of its slowest component.

## Common Implementations

### Bounded Queues

The producer writes items to a queue with a fixed maximum capacity. Once the queue is full, the producer blocks (waits) until the consumer drains items and frees space. This is simple and effective for request-response patterns but can introduce latency.

### Credit-Based Flow Control

The consumer explicitly grants the producer permission to send N more items (a "credit"). When the producer has sent N items, it must wait for the consumer to grant additional credits. This model decouples the producer and consumer timing and allows fine-grained control over throughput.

### Reactive-Pull Models

Instead of the producer pushing items to the consumer, the consumer actively requests items on its own schedule (pulling). The producer only generates new items when requested. This is common in reactive programming libraries and gives the consumer full control over backpressure at the source.
